summary: Defines a binary encoding that uniquely identifies Per Hop Behaviors, or sets of them, in protocol messages. It gives Differentiated Services a compact way to name how a router should treat traffic. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 3140.

plainLanguage.summary: Different packages get different treatment, like express or ordinary. This makes short labels for each kind of treatment so devices can tell each other which one they mean.

questions: how to identify quality of service in routing
subtitle: Compact 16-bit codes to identify how a router should treat traffic.

tldr.problem: Differentiated Services (DiffServ) lets routers treat traffic differently (high priority, low latency, etc.), but the DSCP field in IP headers has only 64 possible values. When routers negotiate treatment over management links or MPLS tunnels, they need a way to identify specific Per Hop Behaviors (PHBs) beyond what DSCP alone can express.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2836 defines a 16-bit binary encoding where the first 6 bits hold the DSCP value for standardized PHBs, or a 12-bit code for non-standard ones, with flag bits to indicate single PHBs versus sets of PHBs.
tldr.outcome: Management systems, bandwidth brokers, and MPLS implementations can now unambiguously specify what forwarding behavior each route or connection should receive. This was replaced by RFC 3140.

today: RFC 2836 is a Proposed Standard from May 2000. It was replaced by RFC 3140, which updates the encoding.

sections.title: Identifying Traffic Treatment Behaviors
sections.content:
RFC 2836 defines a compact way to identify Per Hop Behaviors (PHBs), the rules that determine how a router treats traffic at that hop. PHBs are the foundation of Differentiated Services (DiffServ), which allows networks to offer different service levels for different traffic.

In IP packet headers, PHBs are indicated by the Differentiated Services Codepoint (DSCP), a 6-bit field. But there are only 64 possible DSCP values. A network operator can map each DSCP to a PHB, and can define additional PHBs that do not have a standardized DSCP mapping. When routers negotiate bandwidth management or establish MPLS label-switched paths, they must be able to name the PHB or set of PHBs that a connection should receive—and the 64 DSCP values alone are not always enough.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can treat traffic in different ways (fast, reliable, cheap, etc.). Each way is called a PHB. When routers talk to each other about which treatment to use, they need short names for them.

sections.title: PHBs and PHB Sets
sections.content:
A PHB is a forwarding behavior that a router applies to traffic: for example, "low latency for video" or "best effort." In some cases, multiple related PHBs must be handled together—for example, the Assured Forwarding class defines three PHBs (AF11, AF12, AF13) that must follow the same physical path to prevent packet reordering. This group of PHBs is called a PHB set.

The RFC encoding must handle both single PHBs and PHB sets. It also distinguishes between standardized PHBs, which have a recommended DSCP value defined in an RFC, and experimental or local-use PHBs, which are specific to a network operator and must be registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: A PHB is one kind of treatment. Sometimes several related treatments must stay together, called a set. Some treatments are official standards; others are made up for a particular network.

sections.title: The 16-bit Encoding
sections.content:
PHBs are encoded in an unsigned 16-bit field. The encoding has two cases:

Case 1: Standardized PHBs use the recommended DSCP value, left-justified in the 16-bit field, with the lower 10 bits set to zero. For a set of standardized PHBs, the encoding is the smallest DSCP value in the set, with bit 14 set to 1 to mark it as a set (for example, the AF1x class uses the AF11 DSCP with bit 14 set).

Case 2: Non-standardized PHBs use a 12-bit identification code assigned by IANA, left-justified in the field. Bit 15 is set to 1 to distinguish this case from Case 1. Bit 14 indicates whether the code refers to a single PHB (0) or a set (1). Bits 12 and 13 are reserved for future expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: The code is just 16 bits long. Standardized kinds use their DSCP number; non-standard ones use a number from an IANA registry. A flag bit tells whether it is one kind or a group of related kinds.

sections.title: Usage in Networks
sections.content:
PHB codes are used when bandwidth brokers negotiate QoS guarantees across a network, when MPLS establishes label-switched paths that should receive specific treatment, and when ATM switches need to know what forwarding behavior to apply to a virtual circuit. Instead of exchanging a long description of the desired behavior, endpoints can send the compact 16-bit PHB code.

For example, a bandwidth broker might use a PHB code to tell an ATM switch, "traffic on this circuit should receive low-latency treatment." An RSVP or LDP protocol message can include a PHB code to request that an MPLS tunnel be granted a specific forwarding behavior at each hop.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network device asks for a certain kind of treatment (like 'give this low latency'), it sends a 16-bit code instead of describing it in words. Other devices understand what the code means.

sections.title: Registry and Assignments
sections.content:
IANA maintains a registry of Per Hop Behavior Identification Codes for non-standardized PHBs, initially allowing values from 0 to 4095 (12 bits). Assignments require the applicant's identity, a brief description of the PHB, and a reference to a detailed specification. During the first year, IANA forwards requests to the IETF DiffServ Working Group for review. After that, the Transport Area Directors or a designated expert reviews requests.

Modifying a PHB identification code could constitute theft or denial of service, so protocols that use these codes must be adequately protected by encryption and authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: New, non-standard treatments are registered with IANA so everyone knows what the codes mean. The code itself does not provide security, so the protocol using it must protect against tampering.
